column1: P001|A narrow blue line at the dining table|A08|Explore a dining-table composition in which the blue area remains a restrained accent beside a broad grain-like field. The imagined room already has a strong window view, so the object should not compete with every feature at once.|Keep the long outline visually quiet and use the channel as a directional line. Compare the whole table from the entrance and from a seated viewpoint before discussing any final proportions.|Which view should lead?;How much colour feels appropriate?;What dimensions and access need verification?

P002|The console seen from the side|A03|Consider a hallway console whose side is seen before its front. The concept asks how a waterfall-like end could make that approach view purposeful without relying on additional decoration.|Develop the side silhouette first, then compare it with the front elevation. Treat the reference image as an example of an edge relationship, not a proposed construction detail.|Which approach is most common?;What should remain visible with the door open?;How would support and stability be confirmed?

P003|A round centre between two seats|B01|Imagine a low round form connecting two conversation seats. The study focuses on a shared visual centre while leaving the actual seating dimensions and everyday activities unresolved.|Use the circular outline to contrast with straighter room elements. Compare a quieter colour centre with a stronger perimeter accent in a sketch before selecting a direction.|What activity joins the seats?;Which reach and movement questions need review?;How dominant should the top appear?

P004|An entry bench with a quiet front|A09|Explore an entry-position bench concept where the top carries visual interest and the front remains restrained. The intended effect is a calm threshold rather than a display crowded with accessories.|Keep the main emphasis along the top's blue channel and test the silhouette against a pale wall. Record storage and seating as separate functional questions, not assumed capabilities.|Is seating actually required?;What access and movement space matters?;Which functional claims need a confirmed specification?

P005|A console aligned with a wall composition|B09|Imagine a console below an existing wall piece, with alignment chosen around the artwork rather than the wall's full width. The concept explores one clear vertical relationship.|Compare centred and offset arrangements on the same wall sketch. Use the blue edge reference only to discuss a restrained connecting accent between the horizontal object and the wall composition.|What is the visual anchor?;Which offset remains intentional?;What dimensions and wall conditions are known?

P006|A table with two different approach views|A08|Consider a table viewed from an entrance on one side and seating on another. The study asks how the same top can present a strong first view and a quieter everyday view.|Map the primary and secondary sightlines, then place the colour emphasis where both can read it differently. Avoid assuming the reference scene supplies the actual room or a finished design.|Which view deserves priority?;Where could reflections interfere?;What real room information would change the composition?

P007|A small round form beside a reading seat|B01|Explore a compact visual companion to an existing reading chair. The concept is about proportion and presence, with the chair remaining the main personal object in the corner.|Compare the round outline with the chair's profile and leave the top composition simple. Keep use, reach and surface-contact requirements on a separate list for discussion.|What must remain visible about the chair?;What everyday use is intended?;Which dimensions need confirmation?

P008|The bench as an entry-wall rhythm|B02|Imagine a bench-like form placed along a wall with repeated vertical elements. The study asks whether a long horizontal line can connect those elements without copying their pattern.|Use the elongated outline as the main gesture and limit other repeated details. Compare a centred placement with one aligned to the room's normal approach.|What wall rhythm already exists?;Which alignment feels deliberate?;Is the proposed form intended for seating or display?

P009|A waterfall edge as the focal detail|A10|Consider a table concept whose main interest is the transition from top to side. The brief deliberately leaves the rest of the form quiet so that one edge relationship can be discussed clearly.|Study the continuity of colour and grain-like lines at the turn. Pair the detail reference with a whole-object sketch to avoid treating a close-up as a complete design.|Should the transition appear continuous?;What does the close-up omit?;Which construction questions require confirmation?

P010|A table composed around an existing rug|A08|Explore a table whose outline responds to an existing rug's border. The imagined brief values the rug as much as the new object and avoids covering its main motif by default.|Compare a narrower and broader footprint on the same rug plan. Keep the blue accent secondary until the overall relationship is resolved.|Which part of the rug should remain visible?;What use sets the required footprint?;What measurements are still approximate?

P011|A clear block with a single visual centre|B05|Imagine a sculptural clear block with one concentrated internal motif. The study explores how an object can read differently from the front and side without claiming any particular fabrication method.|Keep the surrounding volume visually quiet and compare the motif's overlap from three viewpoints. Use the supplied cube detail only as a reference for apparent depth.|Which viewpoint leads?;How much overlap is desirable?;What optical and structural details remain unknown?

P012|A curved accent on a small plinth|B12|Consider a sculptural study inspired by the circular outline of a bangle, enlarged only as an idea on paper. The concept asks how a simple loop could create a focal point without a dense arrangement.|Compare upright and angled silhouettes in sketches. Treat the bangle image as a shape reference; it is not evidence that an enlarged object exists or can be fabricated.|Which silhouette is strongest?;What supports the proposed orientation?;What scale would need feasibility review?

P013|A layered object read from above|B04|Explore a small sculptural arrangement whose layers are most legible from an elevated viewpoint. The concept separates visual stacking from any claim that the pictured objects are designed to stack safely.|Compare the visible edge rhythm and the amount of overlap in a drawing. Keep the arrangement's actual supports and intended use open for review.|Where will it be viewed from?;Which layers should remain visible?;What stability questions must be resolved?

P014|An open centre with a floral perimeter|B13|Imagine a circular decorative composition that leaves its centre comparatively quiet while floral forms gather toward the perimeter. The intention is to make empty space part of the object.|Use the supplied round floral display as a reference for the relationship between centre and edge. Sketch alternative distributions without claiming the image depicts the proposed result.|How open should the centre remain?;Which flowers are only visual references?;What actual materials and use need assessment?

P015|A blue fragment beside a neutral volume|A04|Explore a sculptural pairing in which a concentrated blue form sits beside a visually quieter volume. The concept uses contrast between active texture and calm outline rather than identical materials.|Make a two-shape study with clearly different visual roles. Limit the textured reference to the accent area and leave material composition unassigned.|Which form carries the accent?;What connects the pair?;Which properties cannot be inferred from the texture image?

P016|A transparent object against a dark background|A05|Consider how a clear floral form might be presented so its outline remains visible against a dark setting. This is a display-composition study, not a preservation proposal for specific flowers.|Compare edge visibility in a wider scene and a close view. Keep surrounding decoration sparse enough to read the silhouette, then record the actual lighting questions.|Which edges disappear?;What viewing conditions matter?;What suitability and display details need confirmation?

P017|A low object with an offset centre|B01|Imagine a sculptural low form whose strongest visual area sits away from the geometric centre. The study explores asymmetry without assuming it creates a functional advantage.|Draw the outline first, then compare two positions for the accent. Review from several approaches so the offset reads as intentional rather than an accidental crop.|Which approach explains the offset?;What remains balanced visually?;What functional use, if any, is intended?

P018|A narrow upright floral silhouette|B10|Explore an upright decorative silhouette in which the flowers read as a vertical sequence. The study uses a supplied floral image as inspiration without claiming the specific arrangement has been made.|Compare generous and tighter margins around the floral forms. Keep the outline simple and note which details should remain recognisable at normal viewing distance.|Which margin supports the composition?;What detail should remain visible?;What real material condition would need assessment?

P019|A small object with a continuous colour path|B09|Consider a sculptural study where a blue path appears to continue over an edge. The focus is on the viewer following one line around a form, not on a verified construction technique.|Use a simple two-view drawing to show the proposed continuation. Keep the wider shape intentionally unresolved until the path's visual role is clear.|Where does the eye begin?;Should the path continue on unseen sides?;What fabrication questions remain open?

P020|Three forms sharing one curve|B12|Imagine three distinct decorative forms connected by a similar curved outline. The concept seeks a family resemblance without identical size or internal pattern.|Sketch the shared curve in each profile and vary only one other feature at a time. The bangle reference informs the curve, not a claim about the three proposed objects.|What exactly repeats?;Which differences are intentional?;How would scale and support be reviewed?

P021|A floral frame above a quiet console|B03|Explore a wall composition in which a floral frame is the primary focus and a console below acts as a visual anchor. The imagined room uses restrained surrounding decoration.|Compare the frame's position relative to the console rather than automatically centring both on the wall. Keep the supplied image labelled as an arrangement reference.|Which centreline matters?;How much surrounding wall should remain visible?;What mounting assessment would be required?

P022|A pair of wall studies with unequal emphasis|B03|Imagine two related wall compositions, one visually stronger than the other. The concept tests whether a pair can feel connected without equal density or identical content.|Give the first composition a concentrated floral area and leave the second more open in the sketch. Compare the pair as a whole before detailing either.|Which piece leads?;What feature connects them?;What actual dimensions and mounting conditions are unknown?

P023|A horizontal floral band in a tall space|B06|Consider a hypothetical wall study that uses a horizontal band to interrupt a tall, narrow area. The reference detail supplies a colour relationship, not a completed wall artwork.|Sketch the band at several heights against the same wall outline. Keep the floral forms abstract until the scale and viewing position are discussed.|What height relates to normal viewing?;How much wall remains quiet?;Which material and installation decisions need review?

P024|An off-centre memory composition|B10|Explore a floral wall concept with the main arrangement deliberately offset. The study asks how an open margin could carry as much visual importance as the flowers.|Compare left and right offsets against the intended approach view. Keep any personal text outside the first composition study so the arrangement can be read clearly.|Which approach supports the offset?;Would text compete with the flowers?;What original materials, if any, would need assessment?

P025|A wall piece framed by an existing doorway|A03|Imagine a wall composition glimpsed through a doorway before the room is entered. The concept studies the doorway as a visual frame rather than assuming the wall piece must dominate the entire room.|Draw the threshold view and the closer room view separately. Use the supplied room scene only to discuss layered framing and label it as a concept reference.|What is visible from the threshold?;Does the closer view add something?;What wall and access facts must be checked?

P026|A blue field beside a floral outline|A04|Consider a wall concept pairing a broad blue field with a more delicate floral silhouette. The intention is to compare areas of visual density without assigning a material or production technique.|Keep the field and silhouette in separate zones on the sketch. Test whether their relationship remains legible from the room's usual viewing distance.|Which area should lead?;How much contrast is useful?;What material and mounting feasibility remains unresolved?

P027|A frame related to a seated viewpoint|B03|Explore a wall arrangement whose primary audience is seated nearby rather than entering the room. The study shifts attention from a conventional centred wall photograph to the actual viewing position.|Draw the seated sightline and note competing objects in that view. Compare the composition at two proposed positions without treating either as a mounting instruction.|Who uses the seat?;What blocks the view?;What height and fixing details require confirmation?

P028|A quiet border around dense flowers|B06|Imagine a floral composition with a deliberately generous border. The concept asks whether extra empty space can make a dense arrangement easier to read without reducing its detail.|Compare border widths in a paper study using the same floral area. Keep the reference image's original proportions visible so the proposed variation is not mistaken for the source.|What density should remain?;Which border feels intentional?;What final dimensions need discussion?

P029|A wall sequence with one shared accent|A04|Explore a sequence of hypothetical wall pieces connected by a recurring blue accent. Each composition would have a different balance of open and active areas.|Sketch the sequence as one strip before developing individual pieces. Repeat the accent's role rather than copying the same texture image into every frame.|What creates continuity?;Which differences keep the sequence interesting?;What space and installation constraints apply?

P030|A floral detail reserved for close viewing|B06|Consider a wall concept that reads simply from across the room but reveals a small floral detail nearby. The study explores two distances of attention.|Keep the overall outline restrained and place the detailed area where a closer viewer could notice it. Use the supplied close-up as a detail reference, not as evidence of the proposed artwork.|What reads from far away?;What rewards a closer look?;Can both be reviewed in a whole-wall sketch?

P031|A bench along a bright entry wall|A09|Imagine an entry arrangement where a dark horizontal form contrasts with a bright wall. The concept focuses on the first view on arrival while leaving practical seating and storage questions open.|Compare the bench outline with the wall's openings and the path into the room. Keep accessories out of the initial study so the main relationship is clear.|What is the arrival viewpoint?;Which path must remain usable?;What function is actually required?

P032|A dining focus beside a broad window|A08|Explore a room composition where the window view is already a strong feature. The table concept should support that view rather than imitate every colour outside.|Keep the table's colour accent limited and compare the silhouette against the window in daylight and evening sketches. The supplied scene is a visual reference, not a real site.|What remains the main focus?;How do evening conditions change the view?;What real room dimensions would guide the brief?

P033|A round form in an angular corner|B01|Consider a low circular object in a room dominated by straight edges. The idea is to create one contrasting outline while keeping other relationships quiet.|Compare the round footprint with nearby seating and wall lines. Test whether the contrast remains clear without adding a second strong colour or pattern.|Which straight edges define the room?;What everyday use is intended?;Which clearances require actual assessment?

P034|A console at the end of a sightline|A03|Imagine a console placed at the end of a hallway view. The concept asks how one identifiable silhouette could provide a visual destination without filling the passage with detail.|Develop the distant outline before the surface pattern. Compare the end view with the side view encountered on approach.|What can be recognised from a distance?;What becomes visible on approach?;What access restrictions remain unknown?

P035|A tray as a movable visual accent|A07|Explore a room arrangement where a tray-like decorative form supplies a contained colour accent. The concept concerns composition and does not assume food, heat or carrying suitability.|Place the accent in two drawn positions and compare its relationship to nearby books and seating. Keep functional use questions separate from the styled reference.|Where does the accent work best?;What use is being proposed?;Which contact and handling properties need confirmation?

P036|A floral object away from the room's main focus|A05|Imagine a small floral display positioned for a more private, close viewing moment rather than the room's entrance. The concept gives the object a quieter role.|Compare a side-position composition with a central one. Keep the surrounding view simple enough to see the outline without suggesting the pictured plinth or room is part of a real commission.|Who would view it closely?;What meaning should remain private?;What actual placement conditions need review?

P037|A low table between unlike chairs|B01|Explore a shared centre between two visually different seats. The concept asks how the connecting object could relate to both without copying either.|Use a simple round outline and compare colour emphasis against each chair separately. Record each chair's practical relationship to the proposed piece as an unresolved use question.|What should connect the seats?;Which contrast should remain?;What dimensions and reach need checking?

P038|A bench at a change in room direction|B02|Consider an entry form positioned near a turn into another space. The study focuses on how an elongated silhouette is seen progressively rather than all at once.|Draw the approach sequence in three views. Keep the end profile legible and avoid assuming that a visually appealing position is clear enough for movement.|What appears first?;Where does the full outline become visible?;What circulation and access assessment is needed?

P039|A console beneath an asymmetrical arrangement|B09|Imagine a console supporting a wall arrangement whose visual weight is off-centre. The concept explores whether the horizontal object can provide calm without forcing symmetry.|Compare alignment to the wall's centre, the artwork's centre and one edge. State which relationship the chosen sketch intends to preserve.|What anchors the composition?;Which alignment feels deliberate?;What site and mounting details remain unknown?

P040|A blue accent repeated across a room|A08|Explore a room concept where a blue detail in a table relates to one existing artwork. The study limits repetition to two points rather than distributing matching accents everywhere.|Mark both accents on a room photograph or sketch and compare their relative strength. Leave other surfaces quieter until the relationship is resolved.|Which accent leads?;Can both be seen together?;What actual colours and viewing conditions need confirmation?
